line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Be7 Nc3
teaches: A move order can be worth more than the move it delays. Playing the natural central break a little later, after the pieces are out, keeps the same position available while denying the opponent the setup they have prepared against — and a defender who is not on familiar ground is worth a tempo on its own.
explains: Black has shut the king's bishop in with the d-pawn, and White has developed the light-squared bishop and the queen's knight before touching the centre. The central push is still coming and the game usually transposes to the same structures; the value of holding it back is that it arrives when the pieces are already placed to meet the reply.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Be7 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 O-O
teaches: Whenever a bishop sits on c4 and a pawn on e4 with a knight able to reach it, check for the centre fork trick before you castle: the knight takes the pawn, and after the recapture a pawn advance hits knight and bishop at once. It is not usually winning, but it solves the defender's problems, and that is the point — the cost is paid in structure, not material.
explains: Black has castled and everything looks routine, but taking on e4 here works: after the recapture the d-pawn comes forward and attacks the knight on e4 and the bishop on c4 together. Dropping the bishop to d3 keeps the bishop pair and the material is level — what is gone is the centre, and trading the e4 pawn for the pawn on d6 is a poor bargain, because it frees the very bishop Black's opening had shut in.
